title: Underproofed versus overproofed bread, how to tell the difference
subtitle: Reading a baked loaf to understand what went wrong in the proof
excerpt: Underproofed and overproofed bread produce different failure signatures. Underproofed dough tears and blows out on the sides; overproofed dough collapses flat and produces a gummy, dense crumb. The poke test gives a reliable indication before baking. The baked loaf tells you what to do differently next time.
sourceNotes: Proofing diagnostics for yeasted and sourdough bread are well-documented in practical baking literature. The poke test is a widely taught method for assessing proof level.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pressing a floured finger 1 cm into the surface of a proofed loaf. Dough that springs back immediately is underproofed; dough that springs back slowly and incompletely is correctly proofed; dough that does not spring back at all is overproofed.
Bread dough that has fermented past its peak. The gas structure has weakened or collapsed and the dough can no longer hold its shape in the oven.

content.text: Getting the proof right is one of the most reliable ways to improve bread. The
is a quick assessment before the loaf goes in the oven. The baked result tells you what to adjust on the next bake.
Before baking: the dough springs back immediately when poked. It feels tight and dense. It looks smaller than expected and does not wobble when the banneton is shaken.

After baking: the loaf has blown out on the sides or at the base where the seam was. The score may have torn rather than opening cleanly. The crumb is tight, slightly gummy at the centre, and the crust may have separated from the crumb on one side (a 'flying crust'). The flavour is bland and under-developed.

Before baking: the dough feels extremely light and airy, almost like a foam. When poked, the indent stays rather than filling back. The loaf has risen well past its expected size. It may slump when tipped from the banneton.

After baking: the loaf is flat, spread wide rather than tall. The crust is pale and doesn't crisp properly. The crumb is dense and gummy with few holes, the gas structure collapsed before the crust could set. The score may not have opened at all.
What correctly proofed dough looks like

The poke test leaves an indent that fills back slowly, over 3 to 5 seconds, but not fully. The dough feels light and slightly jiggly. It holds its shape. It has risen by 50 to 75% since shaping. The score opens cleanly and the loaf springs upward.
Always underproofed: move to a warmer spot, or proof for longer. Always
: proof for less time, or use the cold retard method to slow it down.
